newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: INTERVIEW-Kegalle sees bounce in rubber.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Kegalle sees bounce in rubber.

text.p: Sri Lanka's largest rubber producing company Kegalle Plantations Ltd said on Wednesday its future growth lay in improving yields and maximising income from its rubber estates.
"Since world demand for natural rubber is seen fast outstripping supply, it makes sense to further enhance our position," Jayan Ratwatte, managing director of Kegalle Plantations told Reuters.
"The price of natural rubber is set to rise due to higher demand after the collapse of the former Soviet Union saw many synthetic rubber factories close down," he said.
Kegalle Plantations accounts for five million kg of rubber, or 12.5 percent of the total output of 40 million kg produced by the 23 privatised plantation companies (RPCs).
Kegalle Plantations, which was privatised in 1995, has 11 rubber estates covering 5,551 hectares (13,877 acres).

The government began privatising management of 23 plantation firms, which control some 600,000 hectares of tea, rubber and coconut in 1992. Government holdings in these companies were sold starting in late 1995.
"We have greatly improved yields since taking over ownership, to 920 kg per hectare in the 1996/1997 (April-March) accounting year, from 875," Ratwatte said.
He said the company has also moved quickly to cement its relationship with smallholders who produce about 60 percent of Sri Lanka's rubber.
Kegalle Plantations forecasts total output to rise to 5.4 million kg in the current 1997/98 financial year, mostly due to improved agricultural practices and utilisation of land.
Government officials say Sri Lanka's rubber output is seen rising to 118 million kg in 1997 after a 6.5 percent increase in prices in 1996, when production was 112.5 million kg.
The company's main clients are Ansell Lanka Ltd, a subsidiary of Pacific Dunlop, Richard Pieris & Co and Dipped Products.

The company, which saw net profits grow by 5.3 percent to 98.02 million rupees in the year ended on March 31, 1997, is expected to see significant profit growth in the current financial year, analysts said.

"We see bottom line growth of at least 12 percent, because even a 10 percent difference in the net sales average will make a 40 to 50-million rupee difference to the net profit," said Channa Kurukulasuriya, head of research at brokerage Lanka Securities.
